claim: The pre-placodal ectoderm is marked by the expression of the transcription factor Six1 and its co-activator Eya1.
source: The pre-placodal ectoderm, marked by the expression of the transcription factor Six1 and its co-activator Eya1, develops into placodes and ultimately into many cranial sensory organs and ganglia.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript (e.g., Schlosser and Ahrens, 2004).

claim: The pre-placodal ectoderm develops into placodes and ultimately into many cranial sensory organs and ganglia.
source: The pre-placodal ectoderm, marked by the expression of the transcription factor Six1 and its co-activator Eya1, develops into placodes and ultimately into many cranial sensory organs and ganglia.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in developmental biology, supported by multiple citations in the manuscript.

claim: Hundreds of novel Six1/Eya1 target genes with potentially important roles for placode development were identified using RNA-Seq in Xenopus laevis.
source: Using RNA-Seq in Xenopus laevis we screened for presumptive direct placodal target genes of Six1 and Eya1 by overexpressing hormone-inducible constructs of Six1 and Eya1 in pre-placodal explants, and blocking protein synthesis before hormone-inducing nuclear translocation of Six1 or Eya1. Comparing the transcriptome of explants with non-induced controls, we identified hundreds of novel Six1/Eya1 target genes with potentially important roles for placode development.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by the RNA-Seq data presented in the results section.

claim: Target genes encoding known transcriptional regulators of progenitor fates (e.g. Sox2, Hes8) require Six1 and Eya1 for their placodal expression.
source: Loss-of-function studies confirmed that target genes encoding known transcriptional regulators of progenitor fates (e.g. Sox2, Hes8) and neuronal/sensory differentiation (e.g. Ngn1, Atoh1, Pou4f1, Gfi1) require Six1 and Eya1 for their placodal expression.
evidence: This is supported by loss-of-function experiments using morpholinos and dominant-negative constructs, as shown in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claim: Target genes encoding known transcriptional regulators of neuronal/sensory differentiation (e.g. Ngn1, Atoh1, Pou4f1, Gfi1) require Six1 and Eya1 for their placodal expression.
source: Loss-of-function studies confirmed that target genes encoding known transcriptional regulators of progenitor fates (e.g. Sox2, Hes8) and neuronal/sensory differentiation (e.g. Ngn1, Atoh1, Pou4f1, Gfi1) require Six1 and Eya1 for their placodal expression.
evidence: This is supported by loss-of-function experiments using morpholinos and dominant-negative constructs, as shown in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claim: Cranial placodes give rise to many sense organs of the vertebrate head including nose, ear and lateral line.
source: The cranial placodes give rise to many sense organs of the vertebrate head (including nose, ear and lateral line) and contribute to the anterior pituitary and sensory ganglia of the cranial nerves.
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Cranial placodes contribute to the anterior pituitary and sensory ganglia of the cranial nerves.
source: The cranial placodes give rise to many sense organs of the vertebrate head (including nose, ear and lateral line) and contribute to the anterior pituitary and sensory ganglia of the cranial nerves.
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Cranial placodes and neural crest originated as an evolutionary novelty in stem vertebrates on the adoption of a more active and exploratory life style.
source: Together with the neural crest, which also contributes to cranial ganglia as well as the head skeleton, they originated as an evolutionary novelty in stem vertebrates, on the adoption of a more active and exploratory life style (Northcutt and Gans, 1983; Schlosser, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Northcutt and Gans, 1983 and Schlosser, 2015.

claim: Defects in placode development underlie many congenital diseases of sensory organs and the endocrine system.
source: Defects in placode development underlie many congenital diseases of sensory organs and the endocrine system (Petit et al., 2001; Davis et al., 2013; Xu, 2013), however, despite this central importance of placodes in the evolution and development of the vertebrate head, they have been much less well studied than the neural crest, and little is known about the gene regulatory networks (GRNs) driving early placode development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Petit et al., 2001; Davis et al., 2013; Xu, 2013.

claim: Little is known about the gene regulatory networks (GRNs) driving early placode development.
source: Defects in placode development underlie many congenital diseases of sensory organs and the endocrine system (Petit et al., 2001; Davis et al., 2013; Xu, 2013), however, despite this central importance of placodes in the evolution and development of the vertebrate head, they have been much less well studied than the neural crest, and little is known about the gene regulatory networks (GRNs) driving early placode development.
evidence: This statement provides context for the study and is supported by the lack of comprehensive studies on placodal GRNs.

claim: All cranial placodes develop from a common precursor region, the pre-placodal ectoderm (PPE).
source: Fate mapping studies have shown that all cranial placodes develop from a common precursor region, the pre-placodal ectoderm (PPE) (Streit, 2002; Bhattacharyya et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2008; Pieper et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to fate mapping studies (Streit, 2002; Bhattacharyya et al., 2004; Xu et al., 2008; Pieper et al., 2011).

claim: In neural plate stage embryos, the PPE is located as a horseshoe-shaped domain around the anterior neural plate.
source: In neural plate stage embryos, the PPE is located as a horseshoe-shaped domain around the anterior neural plate (and abutting the cranial neural crest laterally) which subsequently breaks up into individual placodes (Schlosser, 2010; Grocott et al., 2012; Saint-Jeannet and Moody, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schlosser, 2010; Grocott et al., 2012; Saint-Jeannet and Moody, 2014.

claim: The PPE is characterised by the expression of Six1 and Eya1, which also continues in most placodes derived from the PPE.
source: Molecularly, the PPE is characterised by the expression of Six1 and Eya1, which also continues in most placodes derived from the PPE (Schlosser and Ahrens, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlosser and Ahrens, 2004.

claim: Six1 encodes a transcription factor.
source: Whereas Six1 encodes a transcription factor, Eya1 encodes a transcriptional co-activator that also has phosphatase activity (Kumar, 2009; Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013), and Six1 and Eya1 have been shown to form a protein complex and synergistically activate transcription (Ohto et al., 1999; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Eya1 encodes a transcriptional co-activator that also has phosphatase activity.
source: Whereas Six1 encodes a transcription factor, Eya1 encodes a transcriptional co-activator that also has phosphatase activity (Kumar, 2009; Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013), and Six1 and Eya1 have been shown to form a protein complex and synergistically activate transcription (Ohto et al., 1999; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kumar, 2009; Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013.

claim: Six1 and Eya1 form a protein complex and synergistically activate transcription.
source: Whereas Six1 encodes a transcription factor, Eya1 encodes a transcriptional co-activator that also has phosphatase activity (Kumar, 2009; Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013), and Six1 and Eya1 have been shown to form a protein complex and synergistically activate transcription (Ohto et al., 1999; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ohto et al., 1999; Li et al., 2013.

claim: Six1 can act as a transcriptional repressor after binding to the co-repressor Groucho.
source: However, both Six1 and Eya1 also interact with other protein interaction partners; Six1, for example, has been shown to act as a transcriptional repressor after binding to the co-repressor Groucho (Brugmann et al., 2004) whereas Eya1 is known to form protein complexes with other binding partners including the transcription factor Sox2 (Ahmed et al., 2012a; Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brugmann et al., 2004.

claim: Eya1 forms protein complexes with other binding partners including the transcription factor Sox2.
source: However, both Six1 and Eya1 also interact with other protein interaction partners; Six1, for example, has been shown to act as a transcriptional repressor after binding to the co-repressor Groucho (Brugmann et al., 2004) whereas Eya1 is known to form protein complexes with other binding partners including the transcription factor Sox2 (Ahmed et al., 2012a; Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2012a; Tadjuidje and Hegde, 2013.

claim: Loss of Six1 or Eya1 function in mouse, zebrafish, chick or Xenopus embryos leads to a similar spectrum of PPE and placodal defects.
source: Loss of Six1 or Eya1 function in mouse, zebrafish, chick or Xenopus embryos leads to a similar spectrum of PPE and placodal defects, with altered expression of other PPE genes, decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis in many placodes, compromised morphogenetic movements (invagination or cell delamination) and a decreased production of sensory cells and neurons (Xu et al., 1999; Laclef et al., 2003; Zheng et al., 2003; Brugmann et al., 2004; Zou et al., 2004; Kozlowski et al., 2005; Schlosser et al., 2008; Christophorou et al., 2009; Ahmed et al., 2012a, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies in different model organisms.

claim: Mutations in both Six1 and Eya1 lead to branchio-oto-renal (BOR) and branchio-otic (BO) syndromes with congenital hearing loss in human patients.
source: In human patients, mutations in both Six1 and Eya1 lead to branchio-oto-renal (BOR) and branchio-otic (BO) syndromes with congenital hearing loss (Kochhar et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kochhar et al., 2007.

claim: Six1 and Eya1 are core regulators of placode development and promote multiple aspects of placode development synergistically.
source: These findings suggest that these proteins are core regulators of placode development and promote multiple aspects of placode development synergistically, although Eya1-independent roles of Six1 have also been reported (Brugmann et al., 2004; Bricaud and Collazo, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited loss-of-function studies and is supported by citations.

claim: Six1 and Eya1 play central roles during multiple steps in the development of sensory cells and sensory neurons.
source: Specifically, Six1 and Eya1 have been shown to play central roles, during multiple steps, in the development of sensory cells (e.g. hair cells in the inner ear) as well as sensory neurons, and promote both the proliferation of sensory/neuronal progenitors as well as sensory and neuronal differentiation in a dosage dependent fashion (Zou et al., 2004; Schlosser et al., 2008; Zou et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2012b, 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zou et al., 2004; Schlosser et al., 2008; Zou et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2012b, 2012a.

claim: Atoh1 is directly transcriptionally activated by Six1/Eya1 binding to its enhancer.
source: Recently Atoh1, an essential determination gene for hair cell development, has been shown to be directly transcriptionally activated by Six1/Eya1 binding to its enhancer (Ahmed et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ahmed et al., 2012a.

claim: Sox2 and Sox3 are up-regulated by Six1 and Eya1 in the absence of protein synthesis, suggesting that they are direct target genes.
source: Moreover, the neuronal progenitor genes Sox2 and Sox3 have been shown to be up-regulated by Six1 and Eya1 in the absence of protein synthesis, suggesting that they are also direct target genes (Schlosser et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlosser et al., 2008.

claim: No specific screen for direct target genes of Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE and the developing placodes has yet been conducted.
source: Several other direct target genes of Six1 have been identified (Kumar, 2009; Xu, 2013), but no specific screen for direct target genes of Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE and the developing placodes has yet been conducted.
evidence: This statement provides the rationale for the current study.

claim: This study presents the first comprehensive screen for presumptive direct target genes of Six1 and Eya1 in the developing placodes in any vertebrate.
source: Here, using RNA-Seq in Xenopus laevis, we present the first comprehensive screen for presumptive direct target genes of Six1 and Eya1 in the developing placodes in any vertebrate.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study.

claim: Hormone-inducible constructs of Six1 and Eya1 (fused with the human glucocorticoid receptor [GR]) were overexpressed in Xenopus embryos.
source: Hormone-inducible constructs of Six1 and Eya1 (fused with the human glucocorticoid receptor [GR]) were overexpressed, either alone or in combination, in Xenopus embryos.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The PPE was explanted at neural fold stages and nuclear translocation of Six1 or Eya1 was activated in these explants by the addition of dexamethasone (DEX) after blocking protein synthesis by cycloheximide (CHX).
source: We then explanted the PPE at neural fold stages and activated nuclear translocation of Six1 or Eya1 in these explants by the addition of dexamethasone (DEX) after blocking protein synthesis by cycloheximide (CHX).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: This approach has previously been shown to reliably activate direct targets of GR-fusion constructs only in the presence of DEX.
source: This approach has previously been shown to reliably activate direct targets of GR-fusion constructs only in the presence of DEX (Kolm and Sive, 1995; Seo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kolm and Sive, 1995; Seo et al., 2007.

claim: The transcriptome of placodal explants was analysed by RNA-Seq and compared to control explants which were not hormone induced.
source: We then analysed the transcriptome of placodal explants by RNA-Seq and compared this to control explants which were not hormone induced, in order to specifically survey target genes directly activated or repressed by Six1 or Eya1 in the PPE and developing placodes.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: A large number of novel target genes with potentially important roles for cranial placode development were identified.
source: Using this method, we were able to identify a large number of novel target genes with potentially important roles for cranial placode development.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Several target genes encoding known regulators of progenitor fates (e.g. Sox2, Hes8) required both Six1 and Eya1 for their expression in the developing placodes.
source: We were further able to show in loss of function studies that several target genes encoding known regulators of progenitor fates (e.g. Sox2, Hes8) and neuronal/sensory differentiation (e.g. Ngn1, Atoh1, Pou4f1.2, Gfi1a) required both Six1 and Eya1 for their expression in the developing placodes.
evidence: This is supported by loss-of-function experiments shown in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claim: Several target genes encoding known regulators of neuronal/sensory differentiation (e.g. Ngn1, Atoh1, Pou4f1.2, Gfi1a) required both Six1 and Eya1 for their expression in the developing placodes.
source: We were further able to show in loss of function studies that several target genes encoding known regulators of progenitor fates (e.g. Sox2, Hes8) and neuronal/sensory differentiation (e.g. Ngn1, Atoh1, Pou4f1.2, Gfi1a) required both Six1 and Eya1 for their expression in the developing placodes.
evidence: This is supported by loss-of-function experiments shown in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claim: The findings provide pioneering insights into the GRNs regulating placode development downstream of Six1 and Eya1.
source: Our findings provide pioneering insights into the GRNs regulating placode development downstream of Six1 and Eya1, and suggest exciting new avenues of research for understanding placode development and disease.
evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the study.

claim: RNA was extracted from explants cut from the PPE of un-injected embryos and characterised using RNA-Seq to provide a complete transcriptome of the PPE.
source: RNA was extracted from explants cut from the PPE of un-injected embryos and characterised using RNA-Seq to provide a complete transcriptome of the PPE.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: After removing genes expressed at low levels (FPKM < 1) and annotation against a Xenopus mRNA database, a transcriptome comprising 15,794 transcripts was assembled.
source: After removing genes expressed at low levels (FPKM < 1) and annotation against a Xenopus mRNA database (see Materials and methods), we assembled a transcriptome comprising 15,794 transcripts, and the top 1000 expressed genes are shown in Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This describes the data processing and results.

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) on the top 1000 expressed genes revealed that RNA processing/splicing was very highly enriched in the PPE transcriptome (enrichment score [E]: 43).
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) on these genes revealed that RNA processing/splicing was very highly enriched in the PPE transcriptome (enrichment score [E]: 43), suggesting that RNA-binding proteins and mRNA splicing mechanisms may play an important role in placodal development as has also been reported for the neural crest (Simões-Costa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis of the data.

claim: Translation elongation and ribosomal proteins were also highly enriched (E: 32) in the PPE transcriptome, perhaps reflecting the high rate of protein turnover in the rapidly changing PPE.
source: Translation elongation and ribosomal proteins were also highly enriched (E: 32), perhaps reflecting the high rate of protein turnover in the rapidly changing PPE (McCabe et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis of the data and a citation to McCabe et al., 2004.

claim: 365 genes were up-regulated at least twofold in Six1i treatment group.
source: Using this approach, we identified 365 genes up-regulated at least twofold that satisfied all criteria for differential expression (log2 fold change [FC] ≥ 1; FPKM ≥ 1; FC < 0.5 in un-injected control) in Six1i, 508 in Eya1i and 836 in Six1+Eya1i, treatment groups, while 292 genes were down-regulated in Six1i, 218 in Eya1i and 490 in Six1+Eya1i treatment groups (Figure 2A and B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: 508 genes were up-regulated at least twofold in Eya1i treatment group.
source: Using this approach, we identified 365 genes up-regulated at least twofold that satisfied all criteria for differential expression (log2 fold change [FC] ≥ 1; FPKM ≥ 1; FC < 0.5 in un-injected control) in Six1i, 508 in Eya1i and 836 in Six1+Eya1i, treatment groups, while 292 genes were down-regulated in Six1i, 218 in Eya1i and 490 in Six1+Eya1i treatment groups (Figure 2A and B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: 836 genes were up-regulated at least twofold in Six1+Eya1i treatment group.
source: Using this approach, we identified 365 genes up-regulated at least twofold that satisfied all criteria for differential expression (log2 fold change [FC] ≥ 1; FPKM ≥ 1; FC < 0.5 in un-injected control) in Six1i, 508 in Eya1i and 836 in Six1+Eya1i, treatment groups, while 292 genes were down-regulated in Six1i, 218 in Eya1i and 490 in Six1+Eya1i treatment groups (Figure 2A and B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: 292 genes were down-regulated in Six1i treatment group.
source: Using this approach, we identified 365 genes up-regulated at least twofold that satisfied all criteria for differential expression (log2 fold change [FC] ≥ 1; FPKM ≥ 1; FC < 0.5 in un-injected control) in Six1i, 508 in Eya1i and 836 in Six1+Eya1i, treatment groups, while 292 genes were down-regulated in Six1i, 218 in Eya1i and 490 in Six1+Eya1i treatment groups (Figure 2A and B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: 218 genes were down-regulated in Eya1i treatment group.
source: Using this approach, we identified 365 genes up-regulated at least twofold that satisfied all criteria for differential expression (log2 fold change [FC] ≥ 1; FPKM ≥ 1; FC < 0.5 in un-injected control) in Six1i, 508 in Eya1i and 836 in Six1+Eya1i, treatment groups, while 292 genes were down-regulated in Six1i, 218 in Eya1i and 490 in Six1+Eya1i treatment groups (Figure 2A and B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: 490 genes were down-regulated in Six1+Eya1i treatment group.
source: Using this approach, we identified 365 genes up-regulated at least twofold that satisfied all criteria for differential expression (log2 fold change [FC] ≥ 1; FPKM ≥ 1; FC < 0.5 in un-injected control) in Six1i, 508 in Eya1i and 836 in Six1+Eya1i, treatment groups, while 292 genes were down-regulated in Six1i, 218 in Eya1i and 490 in Six1+Eya1i treatment groups (Figure 2A and B; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct report of the RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: With the exception of c-Myc, all known Six1 target genes from previous studies were present in the transcriptome.
source: As an initial means of estimating data quality, we searched for targets of Six1 established in previous studies (Atoh1 (Ahmed et al., 2012a); Slc12a2 (Ando et al., 2005); CyclinA1 (Coletta et al., 2004); CyclinD1 (Li et al., 2013); c-Myc (Li et al., 2003); Ezrin (Yu et al., 2006); Gdnf (Li et al., 2003); Sox3 (Schlosser et al., 2008); Sox2 (Schlosser et al., 2008); Sall1 (Chai et al., 2006); and MyoD1 (Liu et al., 2013)) in the Six1i and Six1+Eya1i data sets. With the exception of c-Myc, all genes were present in the transcriptome, and most were found in either Six1i (CyclinD1 [ccndx] FC: 7.48; Slc12a2, FC: -2.75; CyclinA1, FC: -3.68; Sox2, FC: 1.2; MyoD, FC: 3.4) or Six1+Eya1i (Sox3, FC: 0.9; Atoh1, FC: 1.4; Sall1, FC: 0.99) data sets, confirming the utility of our approach in identifying direct targets.
evidence: This is a validation of the RNA-Seq approach by comparing results to known targets.

claim: Most known Six1 target genes were found in either Six1i or Six1+Eya1i data sets, confirming the utility of the approach in identifying direct targets.
source: As an initial means of estimating data quality, we searched for targets of Six1 established in previous studies (Atoh1 (Ahmed et al., 2012a); Slc12a2 (Ando et al., 2005); CyclinA1 (Coletta et al., 2004); CyclinD1 (Li et al., 2013); c-Myc (Li et al., 2003); Ezrin (Yu et al., 2006); Gdnf (Li et al., 2003); Sox3 (Schlosser et al., 2008); Sox2 (Schlosser et al., 2008); Sall1 (Chai et al., 2006); and MyoD1 (Liu et al., 2013)) in the Six1i and Six1+Eya1i data sets. With the exception of c-Myc, all genes were present in the transcriptome, and most were found in either Six1i (CyclinD1 [ccndx] FC: 7.48; Slc12a2, FC: -2.75; CyclinA1, FC: -3.68; Sox2, FC: 1.2; MyoD, FC: 3.4) or Six1+Eya1i (Sox3, FC: 0.9; Atoh1, FC: 1.4; Sall1, FC: 0.99) data sets, confirming the utility of our approach in identifying direct targets.
evidence: This is a validation of the RNA-Seq approach by comparing results to known targets.

claim: Atoh1, Sox2 and MyoD1 were found both in Six1+Eya1i and Eya1i datasets as expected based on the known coregulation of these Six1 target genes by Eya1.
source: Moreover, Atoh1, Sox2 and MyoD1 were found both in our Six1+Eya1i and Eya1i datasets as expected based on the known coregulation of these Six1 target genes by Eya1 (Ahmed et al., 2012a; Grifone et al., 2007; Schlosser et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ahmed et al., 2012a; Grifone et al., 2007; Schlosser et al., 2008.

claim: Overexpression of Eya1 alone may upregulate genes in those parts of the ectoderm where Six1 is already expressed at high levels but Eya1 at relatively low levels in vivo.
source: We suggest that overexpression of Eya1 alone may upregulate such genes in those parts of the ectoderm where Six1 is already expressed at high levels but Eya1 at relatively low levels in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some genes are upregulated by Eya1 alone.

claim: About half of all genes differentially expressed in the PPE show evidence of co-regulation by Six1 and Eya1.
source: About half of all genes differentially expressed in the PPE in our various treatment groups show evidence of co-regulation by Six1 and Eya1. This includes 690 (633+57) up-regulated and 444 (440+4) down-regulated genes (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The top 10% of transcripts up-regulated in Six1i, Eya1i or Six+Eya1i treatment groups were each highly enriched for the top 10% of transcripts up-regulated in any of the other experimental treatment groups (p<0.0001; Fisher's exact test).
source: Indeed, the top 10% of transcripts (ranked by FC; post DEX-filtering) up-regulated in Six1i, Eya1i or Six+Eya1i treatment groups were each highly enriched for the top 10% of transcripts up-regulated in any of the other experimental treatment groups (p<0.0001; Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: More genes co-regulated by Six1 and Eya1 were up-regulated than were down-regulated (690/1134 = 60.8% for all co-regulated genes, 57/61 = 93.4% for co-regulated genes identified in each treatment group).
source: More genes co-regulated by Six1 and Eya1 were up-regulated than were down-regulated (690/1134 = 60.8% for all co-regulated genes, 57/61 = 93.4% for co-regulated genes identified in each treatment group; Figure 2A and B), corroborating previous findings that Six1 and Eya1 typically act synergistically to activate transcription (Ahmed et al., 2012b, 2012a; Brugmann et al., 2004; Christophorou et al., 2009; Li et al., 2003; Ruf et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The identification of a subset of genes synergistically down-regulated by Six1 and Eya1 suggests that Eya1 may not always act as a co-activator of Six1.
source: However, our identification of a subset of genes synergistically down-regulated by Six1 and Eya1 suggests that Eya1 may not always act as a co-activator of Six1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some genes are down-regulated by Six1 and Eya1.

claim: 283 (190+93) genes were up-regulated by Six1 but not Eya1, indicating that these are regulated by Six1 in an Eya1 independent way but possibly dependent on other co-factors.
source: We identified 283 (190+93) genes up-regulated and 270 (233+37) genes down-regulated by Six1 but not Eya1, indicating that these are regulated by Six1 in an Eya1 independent way but possibly dependent on other co-factors.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: 426 (373+53) genes were up-regulated and 196 (187+9) genes were down-regulated by Eya1 but not Six1, suggesting that these are regulated by Eya1 in conjunction with transcription factors other than Six1.
source: Conversely, we identified 426 (373+53) genes up-regulated and 196 (187+9) genes down-regulated by Eya1 but not Six1 (Figure 2A,B) suggesting that these are regulated by Eya1 in conjunction with transcription factors other than Six1.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: 181 genes were significantly (q<0.05) up-regulated in the Six1+Eya1m group.
source: We found 181 significantly (q<0.05) up-regulated genes in the Six1+Eya1m group, 149 in Six1m and 112 in Eya1m (Supplementary file 3, Tables 1–3).
evidence: This is a direct report of the merged RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: 149 genes were significantly (q<0.05) up-regulated in the Six1m group.
source: We found 181 significantly (q<0.05) up-regulated genes in the Six1+Eya1m group, 149 in Six1m and 112 in Eya1m (Supplementary file 3, Tables 1–3).
evidence: This is a direct report of the merged RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: 112 genes were significantly (q<0.05) up-regulated in the Eya1m group.
source: We found 181 significantly (q<0.05) up-regulated genes in the Six1+Eya1m group, 149 in Six1m and 112 in Eya1m (Supplementary file 3, Tables 1–3).
evidence: This is a direct report of the merged RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: Substantially fewer genes were negatively regulated in the merged groups, with only 14 significantly down-regulated genes found in Six1+Eya1m, 11 in Six1m and 13 in Eya1m.
source: Substantially fewer genes were negatively regulated in these merged groups, with only 14 significantly down-regulated genes found in Six1+Eya1m, 11 in Six1m and 13 in Eya1m (Supplementary file 3, Tables 4–6), re-enforcing the notion that together, Six1 and Eya1 act primarily as transcriptional activators (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a direct report of the merged RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claim: Together, Six1 and Eya1 act primarily as transcriptional activators.
source: Substantially fewer genes were negatively regulated in these merged groups, with only 14 significantly down-regulated genes found in Six1+Eya1m, 11 in Six1m and 13 in Eya1m (Supplementary file 3, Tables 4–6), re-enforcing the notion that together, Six1 and Eya1 act primarily as transcriptional activators (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that more genes are up-regulated than down-regulated.

claim: Transcription factors and protein binding together accounted for the largest fraction of up-regulated genes (53% in total) in the Six1+Eya1m merged data set.
source: Presumptive direct targets that were significantly up-regulated in our merged data set (Six1+Eya1m) were analysed using Panther (Mi et al., 2013) to examine the representation of genes grouped by molecular function (Figure 2D). Transcription factors and protein binding together accounted for the largest fraction of up-regulated genes (53% in total), followed by enzymes (30%) and transporter molecules (13%), suggesting a developmental function of many of the genes up-regulated by either Six1 or Eya1.
evidence: This is based on Panther analysis of the merged RNA-Seq data, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Genes directly up-regulated by Six1, Eya1 or Six1+Eya1 were highly enriched for terms associated with sense organ development, inner-ear development, mechanoreceptor differentiation, eye morphogenesis, neurogenesis and axon guidance.
source: GSEA was then conducted using DAVID (Huang et al., 2009) on the sets of significantly up- or down-regulated genes in our merged data sets, as well as in various combinations of subsets of differentially expressed genes from our individual treatment groups (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1). This analysis showed that genes directly up-regulated by Six1, Eya1 or Six1+Eya1 were highly enriched for terms associated with sense organ development, inner-ear development, mechanoreceptor differentiation, eye morphogenesis, neurogenesis and axon guidance consistent with their synergistic role in sensory development (Grocott et al., 2012; Schlosser, 2010) and neurogenesis (Maier et al., 2014; Schlosser and Northcutt, 2000).
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of the merged RNA-Seq data, as shown in Figure 3.

claim: Genes encoding cell cycle regulators (CyclinD, RGCC), cell surface receptors and adhesion molecules (e.g. CXCR7, EDAR, Protocadherin11, Claudin3, Fzd1, Fzd4,), secreted proteins (e.g. FGF3, FGF19, Dkk1, Neurotrophin3) and cytoskeletal regulators (e.g. RhoV, Espin) with known or potential roles in placode development were also up-regulated.
source: Apart from genes encoding transcription factors involved in sensory development (see below), genes encoding cell cycle regulators (CyclinD, RGCC), cell surface receptors and adhesion molecules (e.g. CXCR7, EDAR, Protocadherin11, Claudin3, Fzd1, Fzd4,), secreted proteins (e.g. FGF3, FGF19, Dkk1, Neurotrophin3) and cytoskeletal regulators (e.g. RhoV, Espin) with known or potential roles in placode development were also up-regulated.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Hox genes (specifically of the Antennapedia-type) were extremely enriched in the Eya1-specific subset of up-regulated genes.
source: A particularly interesting finding was the extreme enrichment of Hox genes (specifically of the Antennapedia-type) in the Eya1-specific subset of up-regulated genes (Figure 3F), suggesting that Eya1 may play a previously un-identified role in regulating Hox gene expression independently of Six1.
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of the RNA-Seq data, as shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Eya1 may play a previously un-identified role in regulating Hox gene expression independently of Six1.
source: A particularly interesting finding was the extreme enrichment of Hox genes (specifically of the Antennapedia-type) in the Eya1-specific subset of up-regulated genes (Figure 3F), suggesting that Eya1 may play a previously un-identified role in regulating Hox gene expression independently of Six1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GSEA analysis showing enrichment of Hox genes in Eya1-specific targets.

claim: A list of well-supported target genes was generated containing all genes with at least a two-fold up-regulation in at least two of the three treatment groups.
source: To verify our RNA-Seq data, we selected a number of target genes for further characterisation and, in order to gain insight into the GRN downstream of Six1 and Eya1, we restricted candidates to transcription factors or co-factors up-regulated by Six1 or Eya1. First, we generated a list of well-supported target genes containing all genes with at least a two-fold up-regulation in at least two of our three treatment groups (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to select genes for further analysis.

claim: From the 228 genes in the well-supported target gene list, 30 transcription factors or co-factors were selected for further analysis.
source: From the 228 genes in this list we selected all 30 transcription factors or co-factors for further analysis.
evidence: This describes the selection of genes for further analysis.

claim: Sox3 and Ngn1 were included in the analysis because previous studies have implicated these genes in the regulation of placodal neurogenesis downstream of Six1 and Eya1.
source: We additionally included Sox3 and Ngn1 - which were found to be slightly below our threshold of twofold up-regulation in at least two treatment groups - because previous studies have implicated these genes in the regulation of placodal neurogenesis downstream of Six1 and Eya1 (Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Schlosser et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2012b) (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Schlosser et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2012b.

claim: 19/30 (63.3%) of the transcriptional regulators selected for analysis were expressed in PPE or placodal derivatives.
source: We found 19/30 (63.3% ) of these transcriptional regulators to be expressed in PPE or placodal derivatives, while 11/30 (Sox17, MyoD1, Sox1, Ets2a, Mafa, Emx1.2, Lhx5, Pou3f2b, Tbx6, Tbx15, Sim1) were not expressed in either the PPE or any placodal derivatives.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization analysis of the selected genes.

claim: 11/30 transcriptional regulators (Sox17, MyoD1, Sox1, Ets2a, Mafa, Emx1.2, Lhx5, Pou3f2b, Tbx6, Tbx15, Sim1) were not expressed in either the PPE or any placodal derivatives.
source: We found 19/30 (63.3% ) of these transcriptional regulators to be expressed in PPE or placodal derivatives, while 11/30 (Sox17, MyoD1, Sox1, Ets2a, Mafa, Emx1.2, Lhx5, Pou3f2b, Tbx6, Tbx15, Sim1) were not expressed in either the PPE or any placodal derivatives.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization analysis of the selected genes.

claim: Many of the genes not expressed in the PPE or placodal derivatives were expressed in the adjacent neural folds or other tissues.
source: However, many of the genes in the latter group were expressed in the adjacent neural folds or other tissues. Thus, it is possible that such genes may be direct targets of Six1 or Eya1 in domains surrounding the PPE, likely to have been included in our screen as a result of non-PPE contamination during dissection.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization analysis and is an inference about the reason for their inclusion in the screen.

claim: 79% (15/19) of the transcriptional regulators expressed in the PPE or placodal derivatives were statistically supported in the analyses of merged datasets.
source: Of the transcriptional regulators identified in our list of well-supported targets and expressed in the PPE or placodal derivatives 79% (15/19) were statistically supported in the analyses of merged datasets (Table 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the merged RNA-Seq data.

claim: Selected genes were independently verified as being direct targets of either Six1 (Isl2) or of both Six1 and Eya1 (all other targets; Sox3 not analysed) in the PPE by qPCR.
source: Selected genes were independently verified as being direct targets of either Six1 (Isl2) or of both Six1 and Eya1 (all other targets; Sox3 not analysed) in the PPE by qPCR, and the results were broadly consistent with the RNA-Seq data (Figure 4U and V).
evidence: This is based on qPCR validation experiments, as shown in Figure 4U and V.

claim: Knockdown of either Six1 or Eya1 significantly reduced the expression of all direct target genes in PPE or placodes.
source: Compared to injection with a control MO (Eya1-mmMO with 5 mismatches relative to Eya1-MO2), knockdown of either Six1 or Eya1 significantly reduced the expression of all direct target genes in PPE or placodes, demonstrating that both Six1 and Eya1 are required for their expression (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Table 3).
evidence: This is based on loss-of-function experiments using morpholinos, as shown in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claim: Expression patterns of all target genes after overexpression of a dominant-negative version of Six1 (Six1-EnR) were highly similar to those seen after MO-knockdown of either Six1 or Eya1.
source: To control for off-target effects associated with MO use, target gene expression was also analysed after overexpression of a dominant-negative version of Six1 (Six1-EnR; Brugmann et al., 2004). Expression patterns of all target genes were highly similar to those seen after MO-knockdown of either Six1 or Eya1, suggesting that the observed reductions in expression were caused by Six1 or Eya1 knockdown as opposed to being an artefact of MO use (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on experiments using a dominant-negative construct, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Six1 and Eya1 are essential direct upstream regulators of multiple genes encoding transcription factors that promote neuro- and sensorigenesis in the PPE and placodes.
source: Taken together, these findings show that Six1 and Eya1 are essential direct upstream regulators of multiple genes encoding transcription factors that promote neuro- and sensorigenesis in the PPE and placodes.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Injection of Six1-GR or Eya1-GR resulted in up-regulation of direct targets in a minority of cases.
source: Surprisingly, although injection of Six1-GR or Eya1-GR resulted in up-regulation of direct targets in a minority of cases (Table 3; Figures 6 and 7), the dominant observed phenotype was down-regulation of target gene expression in the PPE or placodes (Table 3; Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is based on gain-of-function experiments using hormone-inducible constructs, as shown in Table 3 and Figures 6-9.

claim: The dominant observed phenotype after injection of Six1-GR or Eya1-GR was down-regulation of target gene expression in the PPE or placodes.
source: Surprisingly, although injection of Six1-GR or Eya1-GR resulted in up-regulation of direct targets in a minority of cases (Table 3; Figures 6 and 7), the dominant observed phenotype was down-regulation of target gene expression in the PPE or placodes (Table 3; Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: This is based on gain-of-function experiments using hormone-inducible constructs, as shown in Table 3 and Figures 8 and 9.

claim: Six1 and Eya1 additionally affect expression of many of their direct target genes in indirect and partly opposing ways.
source: Considering that here, unlike in the initial RNA-Seq screen and qPCR experiments, CHX was not used to block protein synthesis, these results indicate that Six1 and Eya1 additionally affect expression of many of their direct target genes in indirect and partly opposing ways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gain-of-function experiments without CHX show different results than the initial screen with CHX.

claim: Overexpression of GR-fusion constructs followed by DEX-induced nuclear translocation in the presence of protein synthesis inhibitors has been previously used successfully to screen for direct target genes of transcription factors or cofactors in Xenopus.
source: Overexpression of GR-fusion constructs followed by DEX-induced nuclear translocation in the presence of protein synthesis inhibitors has been previously used successfully to screen for direct target genes of transcription factors or cofactors in Xenopus (Kolm and Sive, 1995; Taverner et al., 2005; Seo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kolm and Sive, 1995; Taverner et al., 2005; Seo et al., 2007.

claim: This strategy recovers the majority of direct Six1 target genes known from previous studies, indicating its reliability.
source: Here, we combine this approach with high-throughput sequencing of tissue-specific RNA to identify several hundred novel presumptive direct target genes of Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE. We show that this strategy indeed recovers the majority of direct Six1 target genes known from previous studies, indicating its reliability.
evidence: This is based on the validation of the RNA-Seq approach by comparing results to known targets.

claim: In situ and qPCR analyses of target genes predicted from the RNA-Seq screen provided independent verification of selected target genes suggesting a low false discovery rate.
source: Our in situ and qPCR analyses of target genes predicted from the RNA-Seq screen also provided independent verification of selected target genes suggesting a low false discovery rate.
evidence: This is based on the validation experiments using in situ hybridization and qPCR.

claim: The expression of all genes selected for detailed analysis proved to be dependent on Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE.
source: Moreover, the expression of all genes selected for detailed analysis proved to be dependent on Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE, indicating that many genes our screen predicted as Six1/Eya1 targets are also functionally dependent on these upstream regulators in the PPE.
evidence: This is based on the loss-of-function experiments.

claim: A comparison of the data set with recently identified direct target genes of sine oculis, the Six1 orthologue in the developing eye of Drosophila, reveals that homologues to six out of the 12 sine oculis target genes identified with high confidence are differentially expressed in the Sixi or Six1+Eya1i (and often also in Eya1i) treatment groups.
source: A comparison of our data set with recently identified direct target genes of sine oculis, the Six1 orthologue in the developing eye of Drosophila (Jusiak et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2016) also reveals that homologues to six out of the 12 sine oculis target genes identified with high confidence in Jin et al. (2016) are differentially expressed in our Sixi or Six1+Eya1i (and often also in Eya1i) treatment groups, viz. Six1 and Six2; Eya4; Shh; various matrix metalloproteases (e.g. MMP9); Ets2; and Frizzled1 and Frizzled4.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the RNA-Seq data with published data from Drosophila.

claim: A relatively high proportion of Six1 target genes may be evolutionarily conserved.
source: This suggests that a relatively high proportion of Six1 target genes may be evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with Drosophila data.

claim: Without blocking protein synthesis it is not possible to reliably identify direct target genes, presumably due to the existence of indirect interactions with such targets.
source: Our finding that many of the presumptive direct target genes of Six1 or Eya1 are not up-regulated in the absence of CHX indicates that without blocking protein synthesis it is not possible to reliably identify direct target genes, presumably due to the existence of indirect interactions with such targets.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gain-of-function experiments without CHX show different results than the initial screen with CHX.

claim: The findings differ substantially from the study of Yan et al. (2015), which analysed differentially expressed genes in Xenopus animal cap explants after overexpression of Six1 without first blocking protein synthesis.
source: We believe that this is one of the reasons why our findings differ substantially from the study of Yan et al. (2015), which analysed differentially expressed genes in Xenopus animal cap explants after overexpression of Six1 without first blocking protein synthesis. None of the transcription factors in our prioritised list was identified in the study by Yan et al. (2015); and we found none of the transcription factors differentially expressed in their study.
evidence: This is a comparison of the current study with a previous study by Yan et al. (2015).

claim: A second likely reason for the discrepancy between the results presented here and in Yan et al. (2015) is that this study specifically analysed PPE tissue while Yan et al. (2015) analysed target genes in animal cap tissue.
source: A second likely reason for the discrepancy between the results presented here and in Yan et al. (2015) is that, while we specifically analysed PPE tissue (presumably containing tissue-specific cofactors required for the activation or repression of Six1 and Eya1 target genes specific for the developing placodes), they analysed target genes in animal cap tissue, known to be composed of pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is an inference about the reason for the discrepancy with the Yan et al. (2015) study.

claim: Previous studies have shown that Six1 and Eya1 are essential for both the establishment of the PPE as well as for the subsequent development of placode-derived sense organs.
source: Previous studies have shown that Six1 and Eya1 are essential for both the establishment of the PPE (Brugmann et al., 2004; Christophorou et al., 2009), as well as for the subsequent development of placode-derived sense organs (Xu et al., 1999; Laclef et al., 2003; Zheng et al., 2003; Brugmann et al., 2004; Zou et al., 2004; Kozlowski et al., 2005; Schlosser et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2012b, 2012a) but the mechanisms through which they act are poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The continued expression of both Six1 and Eya1 in almost all placodes developing from the PPE, combined with the observed deficiencies in derivatives from most placodes after loss-of-function of either Six1 or Eya1, indicates that they play a role in generic aspects of placode development shared by all placodes.
source: The continued expression of both genes in almost all placodes developing from the PPE (Schlosser and Ahrens, 2004), combined with the observed deficiencies in derivatives from most placodes after loss-of-function of either Six1 or Eya1, indicates that they play a role in generic aspects of placode development shared by all placodes.
evidence: This is an inference based on expression patterns and loss-of-function studies.

claim: Genes revealed as presumptive direct targets of Six1 and Eya1 were highly enriched for GO terms associated with neurogenesis and placode development.
source: Indeed, our data show that genes revealed as presumptive direct targets of Six1 and Eya1 were highly enriched for GO terms associated with neurogenesis and placode development.
evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: The screen confirms previous studies suggesting that Six1 and Eya1 synergistically regulate many genes in the PPE, and that the Six1-Eya1 protein complex predominantly acts by activating transcription.
source: Our screen also confirms previous studies suggesting that Six1 and Eya1 synergistically regulate many genes in the PPE, and that the Six1-Eya1 protein complex predominantly acts by activating transcription (Li et al., 2003; Brugmann et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the RNA-Seq data and citations to previous studies.

claim: There is support for independent action of Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE, possibly in conjunction with other interacting partners.
source: However, we also find support for independent action of Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE, possibly in conjunction with other interacting partners (Brugmann et al., 2004; Ahmed et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data showing genes regulated by Six1 or Eya1 alone, and is supported by citations.

claim: It has previously been suggested that a generic role of Six1 and Eya1 for all placodes could be implemented in two possible ways: (1) By the direct contribution to the activation of genes regulating developmental processes shared between different placodes such as proliferation, morphogenetic movements and neuronal or sensory cytodifferentiation; or (2) by direct contribution to the activation of genes defining the identity of different individual placodes within the PPE.
source: It has previously been suggested (Schlosser, 2006) that a generic role of Six1 and Eya1 for all placodes could be implemented in two possible ways: (1) By the direct contribution to the activation of genes regulating developmental processes shared between different placodes such as proliferation, morphogenetic movements and neuronal or sensory cytodifferentiation; or (2) by direct contribution to the activation of genes defining the identity of different individual placodes within the PPE.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlosser, 2006.

claim: The data strongly suggest that Six1 and Eya1 act predominantly in the first rather than in the second mode.
source: Our data strongly suggest that Six1 and Eya1 act predominantly in the first rather than in the second mode.
evidence: This is an inference based on the types of genes identified as targets in the RNA-Seq screen.

claim: Only a few genes encoding transcription factors implicated in conferring identity to individual placodes were recovered as targets of Six1 or Eya1, e.g. Gbx2 (FC 1.7 in Six1+Eya1i) and FoxI4 (FC 1.09 in Six1i).
source: A large number of transcription factor encoding genes, including several Pax, Pitx, ANF and FoxI genes, have been implicated in conferring identity to individual placodes, or groups of placodes, within the PPE (reviewed in Schlosser, 2006, 2010; Grocott et al., 2012; Saint-Jeannet and Moody, 2014) however only a few of these genes were recovered as targets of Six1 or Eya1, e.g. Gbx2 (FC 1.7 in Six1+Eya1i) and FoxI4 (FC 1.09 in Six1i).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: A large number of genes encoding transcription factors with roles in neuronal/sensory cytodifferentiation but also other proteins with likely roles for the maintenance of proliferating progenitors, the regulation of cell adhesion and morphogenetic movements and cytodifferentiation were found.
source: In contrast, we found a large number of genes encoding transcription factors with roles in neuronal/sensory cytodifferentiation but also other proteins with likely roles for the maintenance of proliferating progenitors (e.g. Cyclin D, RGCC), the regulation of cell adhesion and morphogenetic movements (e.g. EDAR, CXCR7, Protocadherin11, RhoV, Claudin3) and cytodifferentiation (e.g. Espin, Neurotrophin3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Six1 and Eya1 act as both master genes and micro-managers, acting upstream of a GRN co-ordinating cell differentiation in the PPE as well as directly activating terminal differentiation gene batteries.
source: This suggests that, similar to Hox or Pax genes, Six1 and Eya1 act as both master genes and micro-managers (Akam, 1998; Thompson and Ziman, 2011; Rezsohazy et al., 2015), acting upstream of a GRN co-ordinating cell differentiation in the PPE as well as directly activating terminal differentiation gene batteries.
evidence: This is an inference based on the types of genes identified as targets and is supported by citations.

claim: Six1 and Eya1 have previously been shown to promote a proliferative progenitor state at high doses but neuronal and sensory differentiation at lower doses.
source: Considering that Six1 and Eya1 have previously been shown to promote a proliferative progenitor state at high doses but neuronal and sensory differentiation at lower doses (Schlosser et al., 2008), it is particularly interesting that we identified presumptive direct target genes encoding transcription factors previously implicated in progenitor maintenance (Sox2, Sox3, Hes8, Hes9) and differentiation (Ngn1, Atoh1, POU4f1, Gfi1a, Isl2, Tlx1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlosser et al., 2008.

claim: Presumptive direct target genes encoding transcription factors previously implicated in progenitor maintenance (Sox2, Sox3, Hes8, Hes9) and differentiation (Ngn1, Atoh1, POU4f1, Gfi1a, Isl2, Tlx1) were identified.
source: Considering that Six1 and Eya1 have previously been shown to promote a proliferative progenitor state at high doses but neuronal and sensory differentiation at lower doses (Schlosser et al., 2008), it is particularly interesting that we identified presumptive direct target genes encoding transcription factors previously implicated in progenitor maintenance (Sox2, Sox3, Hes8, Hes9) and differentiation (Ngn1, Atoh1, POU4f1, Gfi1a, Isl2, Tlx1).
evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data.

claim: Both Hes (Hes8, Hes9) and SoxB1 (Sox2, Sox3) proteins are known to keep progenitor cells in an undifferentiated state, and must be down-regulated for neuronal differentiation to proceed.
source: Both Hes (Hes8, Hes9) and SoxB1 (Sox2, Sox3) proteins are known to keep progenitor cells in an undifferentiated state, and must be down-regulated for neuronal differentiation to proceed.
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: Sox2 and Sox3 play multiple roles including activity as pioneer factors, which open up chromatin for transcription.
source: While Sox2 and Sox3 play multiple roles including activity as pioneer factors, which open up chromatin for transcription (Bylund et al., 2003; Graham et al., 2003; Pevny and Placzek, 2005; Bergsland et al., 2011), Hes proteins generally repress neuronal/sensory determination genes such as Ngn1 or Atoh1 as effectors of Notch signalling (Kobayashi and Kageyama, 2014; Su et al., 2015; Abdolazimi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bylund et al., 2003; Graham et al., 2003; Pevny and Placzek, 2005; Bergsland et al., 2011.

claim: Hes proteins generally repress neuronal/sensory determination genes such as Ngn1 or Atoh1 as effectors of Notch signalling.
source: While Sox2 and Sox3 play multiple roles including activity as pioneer factors, which open up chromatin for transcription (Bylund et al., 2003; Graham et al., 2003; Pevny and Placzek, 2005; Bergsland et al., 2011), Hes proteins generally repress neuronal/sensory determination genes such as Ngn1 or Atoh1 as effectors of Notch signalling (Kobayashi and Kageyama, 2014; Su et al., 2015; Abdolazimi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobayashi and Kageyama, 2014; Su et al., 2015; Abdolazimi et al., 2016.

claim: Ngn1 and Atoh1 are known to act as proneural factors that initiate differentiation of sensory neurons and hair cells, respectively.
source: Conversely, Ngn1 and Atoh1 are known to act as proneural factors that initiate differentiation of sensory neurons and hair cells, respectively (Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Bermingham et al., 1999; Millimaki et al., 2007), whereas POU4f1 (previously known as Brn3a), Gfi1a, Isl2 and Tlx1 act further downstream in differentiation of sensory neurons (Patterson and Krieg, 1999; Wallis et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2004; Eng et al., 2004; Lanier et al., 2009; Dykes et al., 2011), and Gfi1a and the related POU domain factor POU4f3 (or Brn3c) are required for hair cell maintenance and survival (Xiang et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Bermingham et al., 1999; Millimaki et al., 2007.

claim: POU4f1 (previously known as Brn3a), Gfi1a, Isl2 and Tlx1 act further downstream in differentiation of sensory neurons.
source: Conversely, Ngn1 and Atoh1 are known to act as proneural factors that initiate differentiation of sensory neurons and hair cells, respectively (Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Bermingham et al., 1999; Millimaki et al., 2007), whereas POU4f1 (previously known as Brn3a), Gfi1a, Isl2 and Tlx1 act further downstream in differentiation of sensory neurons (Patterson and Krieg, 1999; Wallis et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2004; Eng et al., 2004; Lanier et al., 2009; Dykes et al., 2011), and Gfi1a and the related POU domain factor POU4f3 (or Brn3c) are required for hair cell maintenance and survival (Xiang et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patterson and Krieg, 1999; Wallis et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2004; Eng et al., 2004; Lanier et al., 2009; Dykes et al., 2011.

claim: Gfi1a and the related POU domain factor POU4f3 (or Brn3c) are required for hair cell maintenance and survival.
source: Conversely, Ngn1 and Atoh1 are known to act as proneural factors that initiate differentiation of sensory neurons and hair cells, respectively (Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Bermingham et al., 1999; Millimaki et al., 2007), whereas POU4f1 (previously known as Brn3a), Gfi1a, Isl2 and Tlx1 act further downstream in differentiation of sensory neurons (Patterson and Krieg, 1999; Wallis et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2004; Eng et al., 2004; Lanier et al., 2009; Dykes et al., 2011), and Gfi1a and the related POU domain factor POU4f3 (or Brn3c) are required for hair cell maintenance and survival (Xiang et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xiang et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2003.

claim: The findings strongly indicate that Six1 and Eya1 directly promote multiple steps during sensory and neuronal development, and act to drive both progenitor maintenance and neuronal differentiation programmes in placodes.
source: Our findings strongly indicate that Six1 and Eya1 directly promote multiple steps during sensory and neuronal development, and act to drive both progenitor maintenance and neuronal differentiation programmes in placodes (summarised in Figure 10), although further functional studies are needed to clarify the mechanism allowing Six1 and Eya1 to maintain the balance between activation of progenitor and differentiation genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings and is shown in Figure 10.

claim: Direct binding of Six1 to regulatory regions of targets identified in this study should be confirmed by methods such as ChIP-Seq.
source: Additionally, direct binding of Six1 to regulatory regions of targets identified in this study should be confirmed by methods such as ChIP-Seq.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The analysis of Six1 and Eya1 presumptive direct target genes presented here establishes a GRN regulating the development of cranial vertebrate sensory organs and neurons from the PPE.
source: The analysis of Six1 and Eya1 presumptive direct target genes presented here establishes a GRN regulating the development of cranial vertebrate sensory organs and neurons from the PPE (Figure 10), and identifies a large number of novel putative direct target genes encoding a diverse array of proteins.
evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the study and is shown in Figure 10.

claim: The data is an invaluable repository of information for designing further functional studies on early sensory development in vertebrates.
source: This makes our data an invaluable repository of information for designing further functional studies on early sensory development in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the study.

claim: Cell proliferation, morphogenesis and cytodifferentiation are also known to be affected in human patients in which Six1 and Eya1 are dysregulated, leading to sensory deficits after Six1 or Eya1 loss of function mutations or enhanced tumour progression after Six1 or Eya1 up-regulation.
source: Finally, while our study focussed on the role of Six1 and Eya1 during sensory development, cell proliferation, morphogenesis and cytodifferentiation are also known to be affected in human patients in which Six1 and Eya1 are dysregulated, leading to sensory deficits after Six1 or Eya1 loss of function mutations (Kochhar et al., 2007) or enhanced tumour progression after Six1 or Eya1 up-regulation (Blevins et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kochhar et al., 2007; Blevins et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016.

claim: Many target genes identified in this study may also be misregulated in diseases associated with Six1 and Eya1 dysregulation, potentially opening up exciting new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
source: This suggests that many target genes identified in our study may also be misregulated in these diseases, potentially opening up exciting new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential clinical relevance of the findings.
